title: “Dancing with the Moon”: Chinese Guqin in Prelude and Fugue No.10, Book II
content_blocks: This combined prelude-and-fugue is inspired by the Song dynasty painting Viewing Plum Blossoms by Moonlight by Ma Yuan (1190-1225), and by the well-known poem Drinking Alone Under the Moon by the Tang Dynasty poet Li Bai (also known as Li Po, 701-762) (translation by David S. Lefkowitz):
A jug of wine, out among the flowers,
All alone, no friends here to drink with me;
So I invite the moon, “come spend some hours!
With you, my shadow and I will be three.”
The moon does not know much about drinking
And my shadow always mimes me, it’s true;
But I’ll be happy enough, I’m thinking,
To satisfy me until spring is through.
When I sing aloud, the moon slips and slides,
When I dance, my shadow stumbles and sways.
While still sober each happily abides,
When we’re drunk we go our separate ways.
Our friendship will outlast all earthly love;
We’ll meet again beyond the stars above.

The three characters are represented by different timbres, recalling the seven-string guqin’s combination of plucked sounds, harmonics, and vibrato and portamento (sliding along the wood from one note to another, most notably in the silent spaces between the notes). Plucking the piano strings with a guitar pick and harmonics are straightforward enough, but vibrato and portamento? Those are tricky!

I came across a special technique completely by accident, when I was experimenting with the piano preparations for Prelude and Fugue No.8 “Marcelle Cahn” (see “A Music Box,” July 23, 2025). For that piece I positioned small bolts between the strings about half an inch from the bridge. But what if they were an inch from the bridge? Two inches? As I started sliding a bolt along the strings, I noticed a faint glissando sound, which would ring out if I stopped sliding the bolt at a node. If I slid the bolt past the node, I would slide it back. But then I noticed that sliding a bolt back and forth along the strings could cause the strings to start vibrating on their own, much as a wine glass will start vibrating when rubbed with fingertips. So I could play the strings like a wine glass, but with control over the harmonics that would sound, and with portamento (glissando) between them. I had turned the piano into a qin!

The prelude introduces the variety of sounds we will hear, leading to a melody that unfolds over a series of three plucked phrases echoed immediately by one of the other types of sounds described above.  This leads to the wine-glass sound, and finally into the fugue, with the subject stated simultaneously in guitar-pick sounds slowly unfolding and keyboard sounds progressing more quickly.  The piece ends with a series of nostalgic “recollections” of the sound world we inhabited.

Recording this piece was a fascinating and frustrating lesson into the potential problems of prepared piano pieces.  When we progressed from my 6’4” Steinway A3 to the 6’11” Steinway B in the studio, I discovered that the extra cross bar in the B’s cast iron frame would prevent the performer from sliding the screws along the strings.  No problem!—the brand new 9’ Yamaha CFXs that we were using for Book I had no crossbar.  But the strings in the Yamahas were so new and smooth that I could not create the friction to cause the strings to vibrate.  We decided that short of moving my piano to UCLA, the best thing would be to record the piece at home, which we did.

But then another revelation. Echoing the Steely Dan line “Even Cathy Berberian knows/ There's one roulade she can't sing,” we learned that even Steve Beck, who can sightread Boulez and is undaunted by the most technically demanding music, couldn’t quite master the wine-glass technique (which I call the “glass armonica” technique). So I stepped in and recorded those parts, while Steve handled the rest. You can see both of us in this video.

One fun fact: as the recording session progressed from late afternoon into early evening, a California Towhee started singing right outside my living room. At first I considered rushing outside to scare the bird away (didn’t it see the illuminated “RECORDING” sign?!), but then I remembered that the Tang Dynasty qin music I was emulating was typically performed outdoors. You can hear it from time to time in the second half of the piece (listen especially about 5’09” into the video, from about 5’49” to the end, or most clearly from about 8’27” to the end).
